clue.text: Line of troops in action

indicators.note: the troops are placed in the action, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a legal action is a case brought in court
RE is the Royal Engineers, a body of British army troops

explanation.surface: A line of soldiers seen in the thick of battle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'action' looks military but is the legal sense, a lawsuit; the troops are the Royal Engineers, a British army corps.
explanation.definitionFit: A crease is a fold mark, a line pressed into cloth or paper, and also a marked line in cricket.

clue.text: An attempt at seduction? I don't believe you!

explanation.surface: A rejected advance met with disbelief.
explanation.definitionFit: A come-on is a sexual advance, and 'come on' also expresses scepticism, as in 'pull the other one'.

clue.text: Hurry back, seizing government vehicle

indicators.note: one piece grabs hold of the other, so the second sits inside the first
going back means the word for hurry is read in reverse

parts.note: to race is to hurry
the state is the government of a country

explanation.surface: Racing back with an official government car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses the word for hurry, giving ECAR, and 'seizing' has that hold the government word after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate car is a British term for a station wagon, a car with a long rear load area.

clue.text: Gloomy bishop opening church bazaar?

indicators.note: the bishop opens up the bazaar, getting inside it

parts.note: a church sale, a jumble or bring-and-buy, is a church fundraiser
B is the chess abbreviation for bishop

explanation.surface: A miserable bishop officially opening the church fete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'opening' suggests cutting a ribbon at the start; here B goes inside SALE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sable is a literary word for black, so dark and gloomy as in mourning.

clue.text: Raids sit uneasily for those like Ann Frank

indicators.note: things sitting uneasily are unsettled, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Raids made people sit uneasily, as recorded by wartime diary writers like Anne Frank.
explanation.definitionFit: Anne Frank kept a famous wartime diary, so she is an example of a diarist, a keeper of a journal.

clue.text: You'll end up suffering, as undertaker might put it?

definitions.meaning: '...' warns that the consequences will be yours
an undertaker arranging your burial could say this literally

explanation.surface: A grim warning, delivered as a funeral director would phrase it.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means you must bear the consequences of your choice; literally, an undertaker's line.

clue.text: Tries to interrupt football team's practice

indicators.note: interrupting means breaking into, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Real Madrid, usually just Real; the 's is the possessive linking to practice
a judge hears or tries a case

explanation.surface: Rugby tries breaking up a football team's training session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tries' looks like rugby scores but means a court hears a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is a practice run of a performance before the real thing.

clue.text: A function I must host in desert

indicators.note: hosting someone means taking them in, so the article goes inside

parts.note: sin, the sine, is a trigonometric function

explanation.surface: A party I must throw in the desert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'function' looks like a party but is the maths sine, SIN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sinai is a desert peninsula in Egypt between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea.

clue.text: Splurge when in Paris at end of June, visiting sister

indicators.note: visitors go into the home of the one visited, so these letters sit inside

parts.note: SR is the abbreviation for sister, as for a nun
quand is French for when

indicators.note: only the final letter of the month is used

explanation.surface: Spending lavishly in Paris at the end of June while staying with a sister.
explanation.definitionFit: To squander money is to waste it extravagantly, much as a splurge does.

clue.text: Rent dockland garage in secret

indicators.note: rent means torn apart, so the letters are pulled into a new order

explanation.surface: Leasing a garage in the docklands under cover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' reads as hiring a property; it is the past tense of rend, torn.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloak-and-dagger describes covert, spy-style intrigue, done in secret.

clue.text: Shelves that you might put in wardrobe

definitions.meaning: to mothball a plan is to shelve it, put it aside for later

definitions.text: that you might put in wardrobe
definitions.meaning: the camphor balls placed among clothes to keep moths away

explanation.surface: A puzzle about what goes in a wardrobe: shelves, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shelves' reads as a noun, the planks in a wardrobe, but it is the verb: postpones.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelving a project and mothballing it both mean storing it unused; the balls themselves protect stored clothing.

clue.text: A believer in hi-tech industry

indicators.note: the answer sits in the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: Someone with faith in the technology business.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu is a follower of Hinduism, so one kind of religious believer.

clue.text: Blooming British abandoning fight

indicators.note: the abbreviation for British leaves the word for a fight, so it is removed

parts.note: a bout is a boxing match or fight

explanation.surface: A bloody British soldier quitting the fight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blooming' looks like a mild British expletive, but it is the definition: in flower.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowers that are out have opened, so they are in bloom.

clue.text: Complexity of speech on European research facility

indicators.note: in an across clue the speech placed on the rest comes after it

parts.note: a lab, short for laboratory, is a place for research
an oration is a formal speech

explanation.surface: A speech dwelling on the intricacies of some European science laboratory, like CERN.
explanation.definitionFit: Elaboration is the adding of detail and intricacy, so it yields complexity.

clue.text: Monstrous female, noted Liverpudlian you say?

indicators.note: the speaker's voice tells us the name is to be heard, not spelt

parts.note: Cilla Black was a famous singer and TV presenter from Liverpool

explanation.surface: Was some famous Liverpool woman really a monster?
explanation.walkthrough: Cilla Black, Liverpool-born singer and host of TV's Blind Date, has a name that sounds like the Greek monster's.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Scylla was a sea monster who seized sailors passing the strait opposite Charybdis.

clue.text: Sleeping topless can be awkward

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the first letter, so it is removed

parts.note: slumbering means sleeping

explanation.surface: Sleeping without a top on can be embarrassing.
explanation.definitionFit: Lumbering means moving heavily and clumsily, so ungainly or awkward.

clue.text: On leave, this writer's becoming unruly

parts.note: someone on leave is at rest, taking a break from work
the setter refers to himself: this writer has, I've, written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A writer who, while on holiday, grows rowdy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This writer' is the setter, so 'this writer's' is I'VE, contracted from I have.
explanation.definitionFit: Restive describes someone fidgety and resisting control, so restless and unruly.

clue.text: Singer doing well, joining Queen perhaps

parts.note: a player doing well is in form
a queen is one kind of ant, the egg-laying female of the colony

explanation.surface: A successful vocalist who joins the rock band Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is slang for one who sings to the police; Queen, the rock band, is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: An informant tells the police what they know, in slang 'sings', so a singer is an informer.

clue.text: Second USA trip fresh in the mind

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters take a new order

explanation.surface: A second American trip remains vivid in the memory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fresh' rearranges USA TRIP to UPSTAIR; S for Second is put at the end rather than mixed in.
explanation.definitionFit: Upstairs is informal for in the head, as in 'not much upstairs', so mentally.

clue.text: Figure Penny has fake army ID

indicators.note: a faked document has been doctored, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man called Penny carries a forged military identity card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penny' looks like a person's name; it is the coin, P.
explanation.definitionFit: A pyramid is a solid geometrical figure with a polygonal base and triangular sides.

clue.text: Improvement that will take you to next level?

definitions.meaning: a boost or rise in standard

definitions.text: that will take you to next level?
definitions.meaning: read as two words, an ... is an elevator going up a floor

explanation.surface: Getting better is what moves you up a level.
explanation.walkthrough: Lift is the British word for an elevator.
explanation.definitionFit: An uplift is a raising of morale or of figures, so an improvement; split, it is a lift heading up.

clue.text: Take care, sweetheart

definitions.meaning: '...!' is a warning to be careful

explanation.surface: A parting word to a loved one.
explanation.definitionFit: Steady on means take care, and going steady makes your partner your steady.

clue.text: Time to meet composer, a nice chap who'll get your tickets

parts.note: Maurice Ravel was the French composer of Bolero
a gent, short for gentleman, is a well-mannered man

explanation.surface: Meeting a composer and a pleasant man who will arrange your concert tickets.
explanation.definitionFit: A travel agent books trips for customers, issuing their rail and plane tickets.

clue.text: Article Time's written about the O2?

indicators.note: written round the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A newspaper article about the O2 venue in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: The O2 is a big London concert venue, so an example of an arena; 'about' reverses ANERA.
explanation.definitionFit: The O2 is a large indoor arena in London, so it is one example of an arena.

clue.text: Perhaps Elizabeth I's governess having change of heart

definitions.note: Elizabeth I is an example; the 's stands for is

indicators.note: the middle letter of the word is swapped for another

parts.note: a governess is a private tutor

explanation.surface: The young queen's governess changing her mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Elizabeth I's own governess (Kat Ashley) fits the surface, but the 's means 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Elizabeth I was the last monarch of the Tudor dynasty, so an example of a Tudor.

clue.text: Proust only occasionally finding time for sexual activity

indicators.note: only some letters of the name are used, every other one

explanation.surface: The novelist Proust rarely finding time for sex.
explanation.definitionFit: The rut is the mating season of deer and similar animals, when stags are sexually active.

clue.text: Old folk freeze at home in retirement

parts.note: to ice something is to freeze it

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word for being at home is read backwards

parts.note: to be in is to be at home

explanation.surface: Elderly people chilling at home after they retire.
explanation.definitionFit: The Iceni were an ancient British tribe, led by Boudicca, so a people of old.

clue.text: Old man given £1000 twice a year

indicators.note: twice says the abbreviation for a year is written down a second time, one copy after the other

parts.note: a grand is slang for a thousand pounds
PA is per annum, Latin for a year

explanation.surface: A pensioner receiving a thousand pounds twice a year.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandpapa is an old-fashioned name for a grandfather, and 'old man' is informal for a father figure.

clue.text: Tsar's egg addled, leading to complaint

indicators.note: an addled egg is rotten and muddled, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: The Tsar ate a bad egg and fell ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a Fabergé egg; 'addled' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The staggers is a disease of livestock causing a reeling gait, so an animal ailment.

clue.text: Quite mean to eclipse Republican

indicators.note: eclipsing a thing means covering it, so the small word goes inside the other

parts.note: petty means small-minded or mean

explanation.surface: A political rival sets out to overshadow a Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretty used as an adverb means fairly, rather or quite, as in pretty good.
